I need to write a JUnit 4 test class for JsonParserSequence, but since Mockito isn't available in the classpath, I'll have to create manual stub implementations of the JsonParser interface. Since JsonParser is an abstract class in jackson-core with many abstract methods, implementing a stub will require covering all of them.

Given the classpath doesn't seem to include jackson-core.jar, I'm assuming the actual project (Defects4J style) already has the source available and I just need JUnit for the test framework itself — no extra mocking library needed. So I'll build a minimal stub class extending JsonParser directly, overriding only the necessary methods and throwing UnsupportedOperationException for the rest.

Instead, a lighter approach might be extending JsonParserDelegate to wrap another parser implementation, avoiding having to stub out every abstract method manually.

Realizing JsonParser has dozens of abstract methods, manually stubbing all of them accurately without the exact source would be tedious and error-prone, so I need a better approach than reimplementing from scratch.

I could instead use a real JsonFactory to create actual concrete JsonParser instances from JSON strings, avoiding the need for mocking entirely. This is simpler and legitimate since JsonFactory.createParser() gives us real, working parser objects to test against.

With this I can design tests that create two real parsers (say from "{}" and "[]"), combine them via JsonParserSequence's public createFlattened method, then verify nextToken() correctly switches between them as tokens are exhausted -- mirroring how Jackson's own test suite validates this behavior.

I also want to test flattening logic itself: when createFlattened receives a sequence as one of its inputs, it should merge contained parsers rather than nesting, so containedParsersCount() should reflect the combined total. I should check this both when the inner sequence hasn't advanced yet (all parsers still active) and after it's been partially consumed via nextToken(), since only the remaining active parsers should be included in the flattened result.

For nextToken() I want to verify it forwards to the current delegate until exhausted, then calls switchToNext() to move on, eventually returning null once all parsers are exhausted. For switchToNext() I'll check the boundary condition at the end of the parser array. For close(), I want to confirm it closes the current delegate then advances through and closes each remaining parser, using real JsonParser instances with isClosed() to verify each one gets closed.

I also want a test using an empty-content parser (like parsing an empty string) mixed with a parser that has real tokens, to confirm nextToken() correctly skips over the empty one and returns the next parser's token, and that a sequence of only empty parsers returns null overall.

I should also verify boundary behavior when advancing a sequence past its last parser—confirming addFlattenedActiveParsers only includes remaining active sub-parsers after some have been consumed, not the ones already exhausted. I'll set up a helper for creating a JsonParser from a JSON string using JsonFactory, then structure the test class around that.

I realize placing the test in the same package (com.fasterxml.jackson.core.util) lets me access protected fields like _parsers and _nextParser, plus protected methods like switchToNext() and addFlattenedActiveParsers(), which enables more thorough whitebox testing without relying solely on real parsing scenarios.

Now I'm sketching out the actual test cases: verifying constructor behavior and containedParsersCount by building parser arrays from real JsonFactory instances, then checking counts after createFlattened calls in both simple and nested sequence scenarios.

For the flattening test, I want to build an inner sequence with two parsers where both are considered active (nextParser at the initial position), then wrap it with a third parser via createFlattened and confirm the outer sequence properly flattens to three parsers total rather than nesting the sequence inside itself.

Then for the partially-consumed case, I need to advance the inner sequence by calling nextToken once so its internal pointer moves past the first parser, then flatten it with a third parser and verify only the remaining active parsers (the second and third) get included since the first was already consumed.

For the nested-within-nested case, I'm realizing createFlattened always flattens fully at construction time, so nesting a JsonParserSequence inside another via the public API just collapses into one flat array anyway — meaning true nested unflattened structures can't really be produced this way.

Now for the basic switch test, I'm setting up p1 with a single int token "1" then null, and p2 with "2", flattening them into seq, and checking that the first nextToken() call returns VALUE_NUMBER_INT from p1 with the correct int value.

Then I continue: the second nextToken() call exhausts p1 and switches to p2, returning VALUE_NUMBER_INT with value 2, while a third call exhausts p2 and returns null since there are no more parsers - I'll assert this and check the internal parser index reaches the array boundary.

For the empty parser skip test, I'm setting up p1 with empty content so its first nextToken() immediately returns null, followed by p2 with actual content to verify the flattening logic correctly skips over exhausted parsers.

I also want a boundary test that directly exercises switchToNext() via package access - checking it returns true and advances the internal index when a next parser exists, then returns false without changing the delegate once the index reaches the parser array length.

Finally, I'm writing a close test with three real parsers, nesting flattened sequences (two parsers inside one, combined with a third), calling close() on the outer sequence, and asserting all three underlying parsers report closed via isClosed().

Confirms the single-element case terminates the loop correctly on the boundary check. I'm also weighing whether other tests, like checking initial null token state or null-input handling for createFlattened, are worth including but they seem less informative and might be skipped.

Actually, since `null instanceof X` always evaluates false, passing null for first or second still routes through the simple non-sequence branch, potentially deferring the NullPointerException to the delegate constructor instead of failing fast at creation. This seems like a legitimate fault-detecting boundary test worth adding: verifying that null-first construction throws NPE from the underlying delegate assignment.

I'll also test passing null as the second parser to createFlattened, confirming containedParsersCount() equals 2 and that eventually invoking nextToken() on the null delegate throws NPE — a legitimate derived behavior. I could also consider an empty-array edge case, but that would require bypassing the public API since createFlattened mandates two arguments.

Since the constructor is package-accessible, constructing a JsonParserSequence directly with an empty array would throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException immediately, since the superclass call indexes into parsers[0] — that's a solid boundary test derived straight from the source. I'll also verify nextToken() behaves correctly when the first delegate isn't exhausted, returning the token immediately without switching — already covered by an earlier test. As for nested flattening where an element is itself a JsonParserSequence, that can't actually happen since createFlattened always flattens fully.

But I realize I can bypass createFlattened by constructing directly with the package-visible constructor, passing in an array that includes a nested JsonParserSequence element without flattening it first. Then I can call addFlattenedActiveParsers() directly since it's accessible in the same package, which exercises the recursive branch that checks if an element is itself a JsonParserSequence. I'm setting up a test where I build a nested sequence from two parsers, wrap it with a third parser into an outer sequence via direct construction, then call addFlattenedActiveParsers to confirm it recursively flattens the nested structure correctly.

I also want a variant where the nested sequence is partially consumed so only its remaining active parser gets included in the flattened result, verifying the recursion respects the current parser index rather than including everything.

Now I'm mapping out the full branch matrix for createFlattened's if-else logic: covering cases where only the first argument is a sequence, only the second is, both are, and neither is, to make sure every combination gets its own dedicated test.

For token access, I'm deciding it's safe to skip an explicit assertion that getCurrentToken() returns null before any token is read, since that's standard documented Jackson behavior and not worth the extra risk of assumption. I'm now setting up a shared JsonFactory and a helper method to construct a JsonParser from a string of test content for reuse across the test suite.

Now I'm confirming the necessary imports needed for the test class, including IOException, List/ArrayList, and the Jackson core classes, and noting that nextToken() throws IOException so the test methods need to declare that. I'm also verifying that isClosed() and getIntValue() are legitimate Jackson API methods safe to call, and double-checking how nextToken() behaves on an empty string input to make sure it returns null at EOF rather than throwing.

Writing the test file...

Same-package access means fields like _nextParser and _parsers are also reachable directly. I'll decide whether to include an explicit import for JsonParserSequence even though it's in the same package—technically redundant but harmless, so I'll add it for clarity as requested.

Now I'm assembling the full test file, numbering each test case and writing comments that map precisely to the branch logic in createFlattened, covering both the simple instanceof check and the nested if/else paths.

I'm working through nextToken's return branches, close's do-while loop, and switchToNext's boundary check, making sure each takes both true and false paths across the test suite, then writing the actual JUnit assertions.

I decided to skip ExpectedException and stick with try/catch plus fail() for exception tests, since that's simpler and stays compatible across all the JUnit jar versions listed, including 4.8.2. Now finalizing the complete test class.
